description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

In this section (maximum 1000 words), please provide a global overview of the project progress **per output**. To what extent have they been achieved? Comment on the activities that have taken place and the most important milestones.

actual.value:
The TMT set the goal of reaching the following 6 outcomes of the training:
1. Increased capacity to work with satellite-derived data, 2. Increased capacity to build conduct analysis based on remote sensing data, 3. Increased capacity on morphological monitoring and hydrological monitoring, 4. Increased capacity to access and work with open-access geodata, 5. Enhanced uptake of cloud-computing / geoprocessing with GEE in daily work, 6. Enhanced ability to incorporate satellite data in the Agri-Water Nexus.
All outcomes were reached. Extra mentioning on the two last outcomes: We indicated and enhanced uptake of cloud-computing / geoprocessing the GEE in the daily work of the participants. During the course we had discussion on this. In the final survey it was clearly indicated by the participants that more time to practice is needed as well as a community to share experiences with and to discuss with. Measures we have taken to enhance this outcome is:
- Set up a Zalo (‘Vietnamese Whats App’) chat group for easy communication amongst the participants and trainers. - Share the knowledge and experience during a final symposium. Where the former vice-rector of HUNRE Prof. Dr. Pham Quy Nhan and the First Secretary of the Dutch embassy (Laurent Umans) underlined the importaonce of enhancing the knowledge on remote sensing and cloud-computing techniques. - Tight connections with the ICP OKP Climate Proof Vietnam project to further work out the TMT training into a course fitting in the curriculum of HUNRE students. - The enhanced ability to incorporate satellite data in the Agri-Water Nexus was clearly shown by the participants working on self-assignments focussing on various themes in the Agri-Water Nexus. Examples of these self-assignments are: - Analysing flood prone shrimp farms in central Vietnam. - Applying agricultural drought indicators for whole of Vietnam. - Analysis the flood damage of agricultural areas and validating the results with crowd sourced information. - Analysing amounts of (heavy) rainfall and comparing with satellite retrieved flood extents.
To work on these self-assignments participants clearly have demonstrated a good capability on outcome 1 to 4.

comment.narrative: E-learning facility attendance list counting participatio n and completion of training course and gender

15-07-2022: In total, 29 people registered for the training. 4 participants dropped out after the first session. On average, 25 participants joined regularly the 12 online sessions – often it was indicated to miss a lecture due to planned meetings of lecturing at their own universities. The online training period was followed by an in-country (in-class) training week. During this week we had 13 participants. This was partially due to the fact that not all participants live in Hanoi, making it difficult for to join the in-class training. This training week had to be postponed from February to May 2022 due to the COVID 19 restrictions. The number of participants during the online training was a lot higher than planned. As the training was online, it was no problem to add these participants without a drop in quality of the training. During the in-country training week we had 13 participants (2 less than the target value). For participants from Ho Chi Minh it was not possible to join and other participants (Thuy Loi University) indicated that they could not combine their lecturing with the travel time to the HUNRE campus.
For the disaggregation. We had 25 participants during the online training period (13M/12F), and 13 participants during the in-country week (5M, 8F).

title.narrative: B.I.6. Number of stimulating measures/extra facilities aimed at preparation, supervision and aftercare of female candidates

comment.narrative: One female staff member of HUNRE will have an exemplary role in the training. Also, we recognise that gender equality goes beyond equal participatio n numbers and are committed to co designing a welcoming and inclusive course that contributes to providing equal opportunitie s for everyone.

15-07-2022: When inviting the participants, we made sure to invite all female staff, and tried to take teaching schedules into account. By organising most of the training online, female participants were able to combine duties at home with the training. Furthermore, during the self-assignment period, participants were able to request help from their mentor whenever it suited them. In this way, female participants could choose when to work on the assignment, making it easier to combine with their other duties at work and at home. Female participants were able to ask questions also using the chat or email, to make them more comfortable. They were furthermore able to evaluate the course in an anonymous way, allowing for honest feedback. Additionally, we had both male and female trainers and mentors to make everyone feel comfortable. Also, we tried to give women the stage during the training. During the online-sessions there was a guest lecture by Ms Nguyễn Thị Thúy Hạnh from HUNRE. During the final seminar, both male and female participants presented their self-assignment. Most of the trainers were female (3 out of 4 during online sessions, 1/2 during the in-country week), encouraging other females to join the training and get familiar with the skillset in a comfortable way.
